title: Part 2, Chapter 37
paragraphs: In which the notable adventure of the Distressed Duenna continues

The duke and duchess were delighted to see how readily Don Quixote was falling in with their scheme; but at that point Sancho spoke up. “I just hope this señora duenna doesn’t throw any obstacles in the way of the governorship I’ve been promised, because I once heard an apothecary from Toledo, a man who chattered like a goldfinch, say that wherever duennas got mixed up in things, nothing good could come of it. God bless me, how that apothecary hated them! So the way I figure it, if all duennas, whatever their sort or station, are pests and busybodies, what must the distressed ones be like — this Countess Three-skirts or Three-tails! Because in my country, skirts or tails, tails or skirts, it’s all the same thing.”

“Quiet, friend Sancho,” said Don Quixote. “Since this lady duenna has come looking for me from so distant a land, she cannot be one of those the apothecary had in mind. Besides, this one is a countess, and when countesses serve as duennas, it is in the service of queens and empresses; in their own houses they are absolute mistresses, with other duennas to wait on them.”

To this Doña Rodriguez, who was present, replied, “My lady the duchess has duennas in her service who could be countesses if fortune had willed it so; ‘but laws go the way kings want them to.’ Let no one speak ill of duennas, least of all the old maiden ones — for though I am not one myself, I know perfectly well the advantage a maiden duenna holds over a widowed one; but ‘the man who clipped us has kept hold of the scissors.’”
“Even so,” said Sancho, “there’s so much about duennas that needs clipping, according to my barber, that ‘it’s better not to stir the rice, even if it sticks to the pot.’”

“These squires,” Doña Rodriguez shot back, “are always our enemies. They haunt the antechambers like ghosts and watch our every step, and whenever they are not saying their prayers — which is often enough — they spend their time gossiping about us, digging up our bones and burying our good name. Well, I can tell these walking blockheads that we will go on living in spite of them, and in great houses too, even if we starve and have to cover our flesh, delicate or otherwise, in widow’s black, the way one covers or hides a dunghill on procession day. By my faith, if it were permitted me and there were time enough, I could prove — not only to everyone present here, but to the whole world — that there is no virtue that cannot be found in a duenna.”

“I have no doubt,” said the duchess, “that my good Doña Rodriguez is right, and very much so; but she would do well to wait for the proper moment to fight her own battle and that of all the other duennas, so as to crush the slander of that vile apothecary and uproot the prejudice lodged in the great Sancho Panza’s mind.”
To which Sancho answered, “Ever since I got a whiff of the governorship, I’ve shaken off all the moods of a squire, and I don’t care a wild fig for every duenna in the world.”

They would have carried this dispute about duennas further if they had not heard the fife and drums strike up once more, which told them that the Distressed Duenna was making her entrance. The duchess asked the duke whether it would be proper to go out and receive her, since she was a countess and a person of rank.

“As far as her being a countess goes,” said Sancho, before the duke could answer, “I’m all for your highnesses going out to receive her; but as far as her being a duenna goes, my opinion is that you shouldn’t move a single step.”
“Who asked you to meddle in this, Sancho?” said Don Quixote.

“Who, señor?” said Sancho. “I meddle because I have every right to meddle, as a squire who learned the rules of courtesy in the school of your worship, the most courteous and best-bred knight in the whole world of courtliness. And in these matters, as I’ve heard your worship say, you can lose as much by a card too many as by a card too few — and for a man whose ears are open, a few words are enough.”
“Sancho is right,” said the duke. “We’ll see what sort of woman this countess is, and measure out by that the courtesy she is owed.”

And now the drums and fife came in as they had before; and here the author brought this short chapter to a close and began the next, carrying forward the same adventure, which is one of the most notable in this history.
